name: GoMechanic
epitaph: Fixed every car. Except its own books.
oneLiner: An app to book car servicing and repairs through a network of partner garages, with fixed prices and doorstep pick-up.
causeOfDeath: Its founders admitted 'grave errors' in financial reporting; once investors found inflated revenue, funding vanished and the company was auctioned off.
moneyNote: Funding total ($62M) and the ~$325M peak valuation (June 2021 round led by Tiger Global) are from Tracxn and Entrackr as cited by TechCrunch. The 2023 auction price was never disclosed; TechCrunch reported the valuation had been slashed to about $30M. Rupee figures are from filings; ~₹75 per dollar used for FY22 comparisons.
inOneMinute: GoMechanic made car servicing simple: book on an app, fixed prices, 900+ partner garages. Tiger Global discussed a **$1.2 billion valuation** in 2022.
Outside due diligence reportedly found **inflated revenue and fake garages**. The founders admitted "grave errors" in financial reporting.
It cut **70% of staff** and was auctioned in 2023. The business was later rebuilt by new owners, without its founders.
killerLine: Your numbers are your reputation. **One inflated figure can wipe out years of real work in a single due-diligence report.**

chapters.title: The idea: a trustworthy mechanic, on an app
chapters.body: Every car owner in India knows the fear: you take your car to a garage and have no idea if the bill is fair. In 2016 four young founders in Gurugram, Amit Bhasin, Kushal Karwa, Rishabh Karwa and Nitin Rana, started GoMechanic to fix that. You booked a service on the app, saw a **fixed price upfront**, and a partner garage did the work, often with doorstep pick-up. GoMechanic did not own garages. It signed up local workshops and gave them customers, training and standard prices. It was a real problem and a smart, light model. By December 2019 it had 150+ workshops in five cities and raised ₹105 crore led by Chiratae Ventures and Sequoia.

chapters.title: The rise: a unicorn in sight
chapters.body: In June 2021 GoMechanic raised **$35–42 million led by Tiger Global**, at a valuation of about $325 million. The company said it had serviced over 2 million cars. By early 2022 it claimed 900+ workshops in 60+ cities, including the UK, Europe and the Middle East. An investor presentation from December 2021 claimed **annual net revenue above $50 million**. In February 2022 TechCrunch reported Tiger Global was in talks to lead a new round at a **$1.2 billion valuation**. That would have made GoMechanic a unicorn. Meanwhile the real costs were huge. In FY22 it spent ₹65 crore on ads alone, and ₹2.32 for every ₹1 it earned.

chapters.title: The cracks: the numbers don't add up
chapters.body: Big investors check the books before they put in money. This is called due diligence. During the 2022 talks, an EY review reportedly found **inflated revenue and some fictitious garages**. The Tiger Global round fell apart. Later talks with Malaysia's Khazanah and SoftBank also collapsed. The filed accounts told a smaller story than the pitch: **operating revenue of ₹91 crore in FY22** (about $12 million), with a loss of ₹114 crore, four times the year before. Even the company's own claims shifted: 2 million cars serviced in June 2021, but "over 800,000" in a January 2022 investor update. GoMechanic had been unable to raise money for over a year and was running out of cash.

chapters.title: The fall: a confession and an auction
chapters.body: On 18 January 2023 Amit Bhasin posted on LinkedIn. He admitted **"grave errors in judgement as we followed growth at all costs"**, said the founders took full responsibility, and announced that about 70% of staff would be let go. Investors, including Sequoia and Tiger Global, issued a joint statement saying they were "deeply distressed by the fact that the founders knowingly misstated facts", and ordered an outside investigation. The company was put up for sale. In March 2023 Servizzy, a group led by auto-parts maker Lifelong, won the auction. The price was not disclosed, but the valuation had reportedly fallen to about $30 million. All the co-founders left.

charts.title: Revenue vs loss (filed accounts)
charts.takeaway: In FY22 losses grew 4× while revenue grew 2.7×: growth was being bought with ads and discounts.

mistakes.title: Misreporting the numbers to investors
mistakes.explain: The founders told investors of **"serious inaccuracies in the company's financial reporting"**, and investors said the founders had acknowledged inflating revenue. Due diligence reportedly found fictitious garages too. Once trust in the numbers broke, no investor would fund the company, even though a real business existed underneath.

mistakes.title: Growth at all costs
mistakes.explain: Bhasin's own words. In FY22 GoMechanic spent **₹65 crore on ads**, its biggest cost, and ₹2.32 for every ₹1 of revenue. Losses grew four-fold. Pressure to show fast growth to justify a unicorn valuation is exactly the pressure that tempts teams to dress up numbers.

mistakes.title: Chasing a valuation the books could not support
mistakes.explain: The company's pitch pointed to a **$1.2 billion valuation**, while the filed accounts showed about $12 million of operating revenue. Big rounds bring deep checks. The higher the valuation you chase, the harder outsiders look, and gaps get found. Strong businesses survive checks; weak numbers rarely do.

mistakes.title: A partner network nobody verified
mistakes.explain: GoMechanic didn't own garages; it listed partners. That made it fast to grow but **easy to overstate**. If you can't prove every workshop on your list is real and active, the list means nothing. Investors with board seats also missed the problems until outside auditors came in.

warningSigns: Do the numbers in our pitch deck differ from the numbers in our filed accounts?
Have we ever rounded up, 'annualised' or projected a number without saying so?
Would we be nervous if an outside auditor checked every partner or customer we list?
Are we spending more than ₹2 for every ₹1 of revenue to hit a growth target set by fundraising?
Is one founder the only person who sees the full financial data?
Have we told investors different numbers at different times for the same metric?

lessons.title: One set of numbers, always
lessons.detail: Keep one source of truth for revenue, customers and partners, and use it in every deck, filing and board meeting. If a metric is a projection or a run-rate, label it clearly.

lessons.title: Assume someone will check
lessons.detail: Every serious investor runs due diligence. Write every number as if an auditor will verify it line by line, because eventually one will.

lessons.title: Verify your own supply
lessons.detail: If your business is a network of partners (garages, sellers, drivers), audit it yourself. Visit a random sample every month. Remove inactive partners from the count.

lessons.title: Don't let the valuation set the plan
lessons.detail: Chasing a unicorn tag pushes you to spend and to stretch numbers. Grow at the speed your real unit economics allow, and raise at a valuation you can defend.

lessons.title: Tell bad news early
lessons.detail: Bhasin's confession came after the cash ran low. Telling your board early when numbers are wrong is painful, but it gives everyone more options and keeps your reputation alive.

quote.text: grave errors in judgement as we followed growth at all costs
quote.who: Amit Bhasin, co-founder and CEO of GoMechanic
quote.context: LinkedIn post on 18 January 2023 announcing 70% layoffs (he later edited out the word 'grave').

afterlife.text: Under Lifelong's consortium, with new CEO Himanshu Arora, GoMechanic raised about $6 million in late 2023 from backers including Hero's Sunil Kant Munjal. By late 2025 sources told Entrackr it had annual recurring revenue of around ₹350 crore and was near break-even, and car marketplace Spinny was reported to be buying it. The business survived; the founders' version of it did not.

disputed.claim: EY found fictitious garages and inflated revenue.
disputed.note: Reported by TechCrunch from two sources; the full audit was never published. The founders' admission and the investors' statement are on record.
Entrackr reported $35M at allotment (June 2021); later reports describe it as $42M. Peak valuation is given as $315–325M across sources.

disputed.claim: The $50M+ annual net revenue in the Dec 2021 investor deck vs ₹91 crore filed FY22 revenue.
disputed.note: Not measured identically (an annualised figure vs a full financial year), so the gap is shown side by side, not as proof of a specific inflated amount.

disputed.claim: No criminal case is known to us.
disputed.note: Investors appointed a third-party firm to investigate; we found no published charges, so no wrongdoing beyond the founders' own admission is stated.
Most sources list four co-founders; Entrackr's 2023 report says 'all three co-founders' left.
Reported by Entrackr and TechCrunch citing sources in Nov–Dec 2025; not confirmed by the companies in the sources we read.
